title: Real Estate Is One Asset Class, Not a Whole Portfolio
summary: A developer's wealth tends to pile up in one asset class he understands deeply. This lesson defines asset classes by what drives their returns, explains correlation in plain English, and shows why diversification only works when the pieces respond to different forces.
body:
An asset class is a group of investments whose returns are driven by the same underlying forces. If everything you own answers to the same forces, you own one bet in many wrappers, however many deeds and accounts you hold.

Recall

Q. What is personal leverage, and why does it matter more than project leverage?

A. Personal leverage is the debt and guarantees that sit on you as an individual, rather than inside a project company. It matters more because it follows you after the project ends and can reach assets that had nothing to do with the deal.

Q. What is a liquidity tier in a wealth architecture?

A. A layer of assets grouped by how fast it can become cash without a forced discount: immediate cash, near-cash, assets that take months, and assets that take years. The tiers tell you what you can actually spend in a crisis.

Q. What does builder's risk insurance cover?

A. Physical loss or damage to the works while under construction, such as fire, storm or theft, subject to the policy's exclusions and limits. It protects the building as it is being built, not the people building it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer becomes wealthy in the asset he knows, and that is right. You should make your first fortune where your knowledge gives you an edge. The danger is that the same knowledge makes you blind to how much of your life now rests on one set of forces. Your projects, your company, your guarantees, your home and often your income all respond to the same things: interest rates, credit availability, local demand and construction cost. When those turn, everything turns together. Last week Warrick and Roman sized your positions. This week asks what you hold outside real estate, and why.

What an asset class really is

In plain English: an asset class is a family of investments that tend to rise and fall for the same reasons.

The professional framing groups assets by their return driver, not by their label. The broad families are cash and short-term deposits, whose return is the short-term interest rate; government bonds, whose return is interest plus the change in rates; corporate credit, which adds a payment for default risk; public equities, which are ownership of company profits and their growth; real assets such as real estate and infrastructure, which earn rent or usage fees from physical things; and commodities and currencies, which move with supply, demand and policy. Private equity and private credit are often called separate classes, but their drivers are mostly the same as public equity and corporate credit, with less liquidity and more fees layered on top.

A worked example, hypothetical. An investor owns three rental buildings in one city, a share in a local development company, and units in a real estate fund. That looks like five holdings. Ask what drives each one: local rents, local cap rates, credit for real estate. It is one asset class, in one city, five times. Now compare an investor who holds one building, a broad public equity index, and short-term government bonds. That is three holdings and three different drivers.

Correlation: whether things move together

In plain English: correlation measures how much two investments tend to move in the same direction at the same time.

The professional framing is a number from minus one to plus one. Plus one means they move together perfectly. Zero means knowing one tells you nothing about the other. Minus one means they move in exactly opposite directions. Diversification is the reduction in total swing you get by combining assets whose correlation is below one. Two assets that each swing a lot can, together, swing less than either one alone, if they do not swing in step.

Two facts about correlation matter more than the definition. First, correlation is not stable. In a severe crisis, many assets that usually move apart fall together, because everyone needs cash at once and sells what they can. Second, private real estate often looks less correlated than it is, because it is valued by periodic appraisal rather than daily trading. An appraisal moves slowly and smooths the line on the chart. The value has fallen; the report has not caught up. Sage taught you appraiser bias in Week 16; this is the same effect showing up in a portfolio statement.

Say that out loud now.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Two investments each have an expected yearly swing, measured as standard deviation, of 20 percent. Put half your money in each. If their correlation is plus one, the portfolio still swings 20 percent; you gained nothing. If the correlation is zero, the portfolio swing falls to about 14 percent. Same expected return, less risk, purely from the combination. The arithmetic is in Day 5. The idea is here: the benefit comes from difference, not from quantity.

Rebalancing: the discipline that makes diversification real

In plain English: rebalancing means trimming what has grown and adding to what has shrunk, so your mix returns to the plan.

The professional framing starts with a strategic asset allocation: written target weights for each class, with a permitted range around each. When a class drifts outside its range, you trade back toward target. This forces you to sell some of what has done well and buy some of what has done badly, which feels wrong every time and is the whole point. Without it, the winners grow until your portfolio has quietly become concentrated again.

For a developer the hard truth is that your largest asset, your project equity, cannot be rebalanced on demand. You cannot sell a third of a half-built building to buy bonds. So you rebalance with new money: profits, distributions and fees are directed by the plan to the classes that are under weight, rather than automatically into the next deal.

How the best do it

Large institutional investors, such as major pension funds and university endowments, typically write an investment policy statement that sets target weights, ranges, liquidity needs and who may approve a change, and then report against it on a fixed calendar. The practice a small developer can copy is not their mix. It is the written policy, approved before markets move, so that a decision in a panic has to argue against a decision made in calm.

The Six-Lens Check

Omar's six lenses on assets beyond real estate. Tax: each class is taxed differently, as income, dividends or gains, and in different places; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: a portfolio held personally may be reachable by project creditors through your guarantees, so where it sits matters. Banking: lenders value liquid assets on a personal statement, often more than another illiquid property. Governance: a written policy states who decides, so changes are deliberate. Estate: liquid, divisible assets are far easier to pass on fairly than a share of one building. Exit: assets outside the business give you the choice to wait for a good exit instead of selling into a bad market.

A licensed adviser is required before you act. This lesson teaches concepts; it recommends no product, fund or security.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is false diversification: many holdings that all respond to the same forces, which look safe in good years and fall together in bad ones. The control is to list every holding, including your company and your guarantees, next to its return driver, and count drivers rather than holdings.

The beginner's mistake

Treating a second, third and fourth property as diversification because they are in different buildings, or relying on a smooth appraisal-based return line as proof that real estate is low risk.

Callback

In Week 7, Warrick asked you to draw your personal balance sheet and set a liquidity floor. That floor only holds if the assets inside it do not collapse at the same moment your projects do. Asset classes with different drivers are how a liquidity floor survives the scenario it was built for.

Recap

An asset class is defined by what drives its return. Correlation measures whether two assets move together, and it rises in a crisis. Diversification comes from difference, not from count, and rebalancing, usually with new money for a developer, keeps the plan from drifting back into concentration.

Next: Ford, with Roman, on Failure Forensics: the Madoff fraud and what fees, custody and conflicts should have told investors.
checklist: I have listed every holding, including my company and guarantees, beside its return driver.
I count drivers, not holdings, when I judge diversification.
I know which of my assets are valued by appraisal and therefore look smoother than they are.
I have written target weights and ranges for each asset class.
Profits and distributions are directed by the plan, not automatically into the next deal.
I have asked what falls together in a severe credit crisis.
A licensed adviser has reviewed the policy before I act on it.
head: Field checklist
speak: An asset class is a group of investments driven by the same forces. Cash follows short-term interest rates, bonds follow rates and credit, public equity follows company profits, and real estate follows rent, cap rates and credit. Correlation measures whether two assets move together, from minus one to plus one. Diversification is the drop in total swing you get by combining assets that do not move in step. Two traps matter. Correlations rise in a crisis, because everyone sells at once. And private real estate is valued by appraisal, so it looks smoother than it is. A developer's wealth naturally piles into one class he understands, and his company, guarantees and home often answer to the same forces. The answer is a written allocation with target weights and ranges, and rebalancing, which for a developer usually means directing new money, not selling buildings. A licensed adviser reviews it before I act.
terms: Asset class — a family of investments whose returns are driven by the same underlying forces.
Correlation — a number from minus one to plus one measuring how much two investments move together.
Rebalancing — trading back toward written target weights when the mix drifts outside its permitted range.

hostile.q: Your personal statement shows eight assets. Seven are property interests in the same city and the eighth is your operating company. Why should I count that as diversified?
hostile.a: You should not, and I do not. I count return drivers, not holdings, and on that count I hold one. My plan is a written target for assets outside real estate, funded from distributions rather than by selling buildings, with ranges and a review date. I can show you the policy and the timetable for getting there.

title: Madoff: When the Manager, the Custodian and the Auditor Were One Story
summary: The Bernard L. Madoff fraud, exposed in December 2008, took investors' money for decades behind steady reported returns. Taken through seven steps, it is a lesson in conflicts of interest, self-custody, and returns too smooth to be true.
rule: Rule 87: Never invest where the manager, the custodian and the record keeper are the same party or under the same control; require independent custody and an auditor you have checked yourself.
body:
The Madoff fraud did not hide in complexity. It hid in a structure where one firm managed the money, held the money and produced the statements about the money, and investors accepted that because the returns were pleasant.

Recall

Q. What does concentration mean in personal capital allocation?

A. Holding so much of your wealth in one asset, sponsor or risk driver that a single failure would change your life. It is measured as a share of net worth, not as a dollar amount.

Q. Why hold a currency reserve in a wealth architecture?

A. To match future spending and obligations in the currency they will be paid in, so a devaluation does not turn a comfortable balance sheet into a shortfall.

Q. What is a waiver of subrogation?

A. A clause in which a party gives up its insurer's right to recover a paid loss from another party to the contract, so that insurers do not sue the project's own team after a covered loss.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, Roman joins me today because this case is about wealth outside real estate, exactly the money you will one day place with someone else. You will not be defrauded by a stranger in a back room. If it happens, it will be by someone respected, referred by people you trust, offering something calm and sensible. That is the shape this fraud had. The facts below are from the public record; where I am not certain of a figure, I describe it without the number.

1. Timeline

Bernard Madoff ran a respected securities firm in New York, Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities, which included a market-making business and, alongside it, an investment advisory operation. For many years the advisory side reported steady, modest gains, month after month, with very few losing months. Money arrived directly and through feeder funds: other managers who placed their clients' money with Madoff and charged their own fees for doing so. From 2000 onward, an analyst named Harry Markopolos sent the United States Securities and Exchange Commission repeated warnings, including a detailed 2005 memo arguing the returns could not be real. Examinations followed and did not uncover the fraud. In late 2008, during the financial crisis, investors asked for their money back faster than new money arrived. On December 11, 2008, Madoff was arrested after telling family members the business was a fraud. He pleaded guilty in March 2009 and was sentenced in June 2009 to 150 years in prison. He died in prison in 2021.

2. Key decisions

The decisive choices were made by investors and intermediaries, not only by Madoff. Investors accepted that the same firm would act as manager, as broker executing the trades, and as custodian holding the assets. Feeder funds chose to pass money through without independently confirming that the assets existed. Investors accepted a small, little-known accounting firm as the auditor of a very large operation.

3. Assumptions

Investors assumed that a long record and a famous name meant someone had checked. They assumed regulators had looked. They assumed that because the strategy was described in plain words, it was being carried out. Each assumption replaced verification with reputation.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

Feeder funds earned fees on the reported returns, so their income depended on the returns continuing, not on confirming them. Investors enjoyed the smooth gains and had no reason to ask hard questions while statements looked good. Madoff needed new money to pay redemptions, so every new investor deepened the hole. Nobody in the chain was paid to be suspicious.

5. Warning signs ignored

Roman's list. The returns were too smooth for the strategy described; they showed little relationship to market swings, which is exactly what real exposure to markets cannot produce. Day 1 taught correlation; here a correlation that was implausibly low was the alarm. The firm held its own clients' assets. The auditor was tiny relative to the money involved. Trading confirmations arrived on paper rather than through independent electronic records. Some sophisticated firms reviewed the operation, could not reconcile it and declined to invest. An analyst put his concerns in writing to the regulator, more than once.

6. Point of no return

For an individual investor, the point of no return was the moment they wired money into a structure where no independent party could confirm the assets existed. After that, safety depended entirely on one person's honesty. For the fraud itself, the end came in 2008, when withdrawals during the crisis exceeded new money and the payments could no longer be made. The crisis did not cause the fraud; it revealed it.

7. Root cause

The root cause, for investors, was a conflict of interest built into the structure: the party reporting the results also controlled the assets and the records. Every other control, the reputation, the referral, the audit letter, sat downstream of that single point of failure. Fees made it worse, because each intermediary earned money for not asking.

What Roman would check today

Roman turns the case into a short due diligence routine you can run on any manager, large or small. First, ask for the name of the custodian and contact it yourself, through a number you find independently, to confirm the account exists in your name. Second, ask who the fund administrator is: the independent firm that calculates the fund's value and sends statements. Third, look up the auditor and ask whether it audits other operations of similar size. Fourth, ask for the strategy in enough detail that someone who did not sell it to you could judge whether the returns are possible. Fifth, compare the return pattern with the markets the strategy claims to trade; a line with almost no bad months, from a strategy that should have them, is a question. Sixth, ask how the manager handles a request to withdraw money, and how fast.

None of this requires expertise in finance. It requires the same instinct you would apply to a contractor who asked to be paid in advance and certify his own progress. On a building site you would never let the party being paid also inspect the work and sign the certificate. The same separation applies to money. Week 83 made the point with independent reviews: a check is only a check if the checker answers to someone other than the person checked.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is trusting a person instead of a structure. The control is separation: the manager decides, an independent custodian holds the assets in your name, an independent administrator or record keeper produces the statements, and a recognised auditor whose standing you have checked reviews it. If any two of those are the same party, you ask why and you usually walk away.

The beginner's mistake

Reading steady returns as proof of skill. Smooth results from an investment that claims market exposure are a question, not a comfort. Ask what would have to be true for the line to be that smooth.

The prevention rule

Rule 87: Never invest where the manager, the custodian and the record keeper are the same party or under the same control; require independent custody and an auditor you have checked yourself.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught the outside view: before trusting a forecast, ask how often things of this kind turn out as promised. A return stream with almost no bad months, from a strategy that should have them, fails the outside view at once. Week 72 added source-of-funds and know-your-client discipline; this case reverses it, asking you to know your manager as thoroughly as a bank must know you.

Recap

Madoff's firm managed, executed, held and reported the money. Feeder funds earned fees without verifying. Returns were too smooth, the auditor too small, and written warnings went unheeded. Rule 87 demands separation and an auditor you check yourself.

Next: Warrick on The Money: how fees compound against you and how correlation changes a portfolio's swing.
checklist: I know who holds the assets, in whose name, for every investment I own.
The manager, the custodian and the record keeper are separate and unrelated.
I have checked the auditor's size, standing and independence myself.
I ask what would have to be true for returns to be as smooth as reported.
I know every fee in the chain, including any intermediary's.
I can confirm my holdings directly with the custodian, not only through the manager.
A referral is a reason to investigate, never a reason to skip investigating.
head: Field checklist
speak: The Madoff fraud ran for decades behind steady, modest reported returns. His firm managed the money, executed the trades, held the assets and produced the statements. Feeder funds passed client money to him and earned fees on returns they never verified. The auditor was a small firm for a very large operation. An analyst warned the regulator in writing from 2000 onward. In December 2008, as crisis withdrawals outran new money, Madoff confessed and was arrested; he was sentenced to 150 years in 2009. The root cause for investors was a structural conflict: the party reporting the results also controlled the assets and the records. Returns too smooth for the strategy were the warning, because real market exposure produces bad months. My rule: the manager, custodian and record keeper must be separate, and I check the auditor myself.
terms: Custodian — an independent institution that holds investment assets in the client's name and confirms them directly.
Feeder fund — a fund that pools investors' money and places it with another manager, usually charging its own fees.
Conflict of interest — a situation where a person's own interest could improperly influence the duty they owe someone else.

hostile.q: This manager has a thirty-year record, a famous client list and a referral from your own banker. Why are you insisting on independent custody and asking about the audit firm?
hostile.a: Because a record, a client list and a referral are reputation, and reputation is downstream of structure. I need to confirm the assets exist directly with an independent custodian in my name, and I need to know the auditor can actually audit an operation this size. If the manager is sound, those checks cost him an afternoon. If he resists them, that resistance is my answer.

title: Fees Compound, Correlation Cuts Risk: The Two Numbers That Run a Portfolio
summary: A fee is a return you give away every year, and it compounds just as growth does. Correlation decides how much risk a mix of assets really carries. This lesson prices both with hypothetical numbers and closes with the Wealth Ledger.
body:
Two numbers decide most of what happens to money you invest outside your projects: the fees you pay, which compound against you, and the correlation between your holdings, which decides how much your combined wealth swings.

Recall

Q. In personal position sizing, what question comes before "how much can I make?"

A. How much can I lose on this position without changing my life or my other obligations? The loss limit sets the size, and the upside is judged inside it.

Q. What are ownership layers in a wealth architecture?

A. The levels at which assets are held, such as personally, in a holding company, in project companies or in a trust, each with its own liability, tax and control consequences.

Q. What is a surety bond on a construction project?

A. A three-party guarantee in which a surety promises the owner that the contractor will perform or pay, with the contractor obliged to repay the surety for any loss.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, in development you fight for a point of return through land price, design efficiency and financing. Outside your projects, the same point leaks away quietly through fees you agreed to once and never look at again. And you can lower your risk without lowering your return, simply by combining assets that respond to different forces. Both effects are arithmetic, and both are worth more to you than most investment opinions.

What a fee really costs

In plain English: a fee charged as a percentage of your money each year is taken from your return every year, and the money taken stops growing for you forever.

The professional framing is the total cost of ownership: management fees, fund expenses, advisory fees, performance fees, transaction costs and any embedded commissions, expressed as a percentage of assets per year. Investors tend to compare the headline fee; the total is what counts.

A worked example, hypothetical round numbers. You invest 1,000,000 dollars for 25 years. Assume a gross return of 7 percent a year before costs. Option A costs 0.25 percent a year in total. Option B costs 2 percent a year in total.

  1. Net return under A: 7 minus 0.25 equals 6.75 percent a year.
  2. Net return under B: 7 minus 2 equals 5 percent a year.
  3. After 25 years, A grows to 1,000,000 times 1.0675 to the power of 25, which is about 5,120,000 dollars.
  4. After 25 years, B grows to 1,000,000 times 1.05 to the power of 25, which is about 3,390,000 dollars.
  5. The difference is about 1,730,000 dollars, on the same money, with the same gross performance.

The fee difference is 1.75 percentage points a year. Over 25 years it took roughly a third of the final wealth. A higher fee can be worth paying if the extra cost buys genuinely better results after fees, but that must be shown, not assumed. The burden of proof sits on the fee.

Say that out loud now.

Correlation in dollars

In plain English: combining assets that do not move together lowers how much your total swings, even if each one swings a lot.

The professional framing uses standard deviation, the usual measure of how far returns spread around their average. For two assets, the portfolio's swing depends on each asset's swing, the weights, and the correlation between them.

A second worked example, hypothetical. Two assets each have an expected return of 7 percent and a standard deviation of 20 percent. Hold half in each.

  1. Correlation plus one: portfolio standard deviation is 20 percent. No benefit.
  2. Correlation plus 0.5: portfolio standard deviation is about 17 percent.
  3. Correlation zero: portfolio standard deviation is about 14 percent.

Expected return stays at 7 percent in every case. Only the swing changes. Now translate it. On a 2,000,000 dollar combined holding, a bad year of two standard deviations below average is roughly a 33 percent fall at correlation plus one and roughly a 21 percent fall at zero, because 7 minus 40 is minus 33, while 7 minus 28 is minus 21. That is a difference of about 240,000 dollars of drawdown on the same expected return, which can be the difference between meeting a capital call from strength and meeting it by selling at the bottom.

Where fees and correlation meet: the hidden cost of looking diversified

The common trap is paying high fees for an investment whose main appeal is that it looks uncorrelated. Some private funds report smooth, appraisal-based values and charge substantial fees, including a share of profits. If the smoothness is an artefact of valuation rather than real independence, you pay a premium for diversification you do not have. Ask two questions of any expensive investment: what is the total cost each year, and what evidence shows its returns are truly driven by something different from what I already own?

Wealth Ledger

Warrick's Wealth Ledger for this subject. On your personal balance sheet, add a line beneath every investment outside real estate showing its total annual cost in dollars, not percent; a dollar figure is harder to ignore. Add a column for return driver, so concentration is visible at a glance. And record, for each holding, how it is valued: daily market price, periodic appraisal, or manager's estimate. Those three columns turn a list of balances into a picture of cost, risk and honesty.

A licensed adviser is required before you act. These figures are hypothetical and illustrate arithmetic; they are not forecasts and recommend no product.

The fee structure of a private fund

Private funds often charge two layers: a management fee on the money committed or invested, and a performance fee, sometimes called carried interest, that takes a share of returns above a hurdle. This is the waterfall Week 38 taught, seen from the investor's chair rather than the sponsor's.

A third worked example, hypothetical. You invest 500,000 dollars. In a year the fund earns 10 percent before fees, which is 50,000 dollars. The management fee is 1.5 percent of 500,000, which is 7,500 dollars, leaving 42,500 dollars, an 8.5 percent return. The performance fee is 20 percent of anything above a 6 percent hurdle. The return above the hurdle is 8.5 minus 6, which is 2.5 percent, or 12,500 dollars. Twenty percent of that is 2,500 dollars. You keep 40,000 dollars, an 8 percent net return. Fees took 10,000 dollars, a fifth of the gross gain. In a bad year the performance fee shrinks, but the management fee is still charged. The exact terms, including whether the fee is on committed or invested capital and whether there is a catch-up, are commercial terms negotiated fund by fund; read them in the offering document.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying for complexity and smoothness that do not reduce your real risk. The control is to price every holding's total cost in dollars each year and to demand evidence, not a sales description, of how its returns differ from your existing exposure.

One more point on fees: ask whether the fee is charged on the value you hold or on the money you committed. A fee on committed capital is charged even on money the fund has not yet called from you, which raises its true cost as a share of what is actually invested. That difference never appears in the headline, so it has to be asked for directly.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking a 1 or 2 percent fee is small because it is small next to a good year's return. The fee is charged in every year, good or bad, and it compounds.

Callback

In Week 15, Sage taught that IRR and equity multiple can tell different stories, and that leakage to tax and fees happens after the headline number. A portfolio fee is the same leakage, running for decades instead of years, which is why it does more damage than its size suggests.

Recap

Fees compound against you: on hypothetical numbers, 1.75 points a year took about a third of the final value over 25 years. Correlation lowers risk without lowering expected return. Pay a high fee only for proven, net-of-fee value and real, evidenced difference.

Next: REGA on The Rules: fiduciary duty, best-interest standards and conflict disclosure, with Two Systems.
checklist: I know the total annual cost of every investment, in dollars.
I compare fees on a total cost basis, not the headline management fee.
Every high-fee holding has evidence of net-of-fee value.
I know how each holding is valued: market price, appraisal or manager estimate.
I have estimated a two-standard-deviation bad year for my combined holdings.
I ask what evidence shows a holding is driven by something different.
My Wealth Ledger shows cost, return driver and valuation method for each line.
head: Field checklist
speak: Two numbers run most of a portfolio. The first is fees. A percentage fee is taken every year, and the money taken never grows for me again. On hypothetical numbers, a million dollars at 7 percent gross for 25 years ends near 5.1 million with a quarter-point fee and near 3.4 million with a two-point fee. That is about a third of the final wealth gone for the same performance. The second number is correlation. Two assets each swinging 20 percent, held half and half, still swing 20 percent if they move together, but only about 14 percent if their correlation is zero, with the same expected return. The trap is paying high fees for smooth, appraisal-based returns that only look uncorrelated. So I price every holding's cost in dollars, record how it is valued, and demand evidence that it really behaves differently before I pay for it.
terms: Total cost of ownership — every fee and cost of an investment, including management, fund, advisory, performance and trading costs, expressed per year.
Standard deviation — a measure of how widely returns spread around their average; the usual measure of an investment's swing.
Drawdown — the fall in value from a previous high to a later low.

hostile.q: Our fund charges more than an index fund, but our returns are smoother and barely correlated with stocks. Isn't that worth the premium?
hostile.a: It might be, if the smoothness is real. Show me how the holdings are valued, how often and by whom. If the values come from periodic appraisals or your own estimates, the low correlation may be a reporting effect. I also need the total annual cost in dollars, including the performance fee, and your net-of-fee results in years when markets fell. If the evidence holds up, we can talk about the premium.

title: Who Your Adviser Works For: Duties, Disclosure and Conflicts
summary: Not every person who gives investment advice owes the same duty. This lesson separates fiduciary duty, best-interest standards and suitability, explains how conflicts and fees must be disclosed, and compares how Canada and Guyana approach adviser regulation.
body:
Before you take anyone's investment advice, find out what duty the law places on them, how they are paid and what conflicts they must disclose. The same words, "financial adviser", can describe people with very different obligations to you.

Recall

Q. What is the danger of personal guarantees in a capital allocation plan?

A. A guarantee is a contingent liability that does not appear as debt until it is called, so it can make a balance sheet look far stronger than it is. It must be counted against your net worth as a possible loss.

Q. What is the purpose of a liquidity floor?

A. A minimum amount of readily available cash and near-cash you will not go below, sized to cover obligations and living costs through a bad period without forced sales.

Q. What is professional indemnity insurance?

A. Insurance for a professional, such as a designer or engineer, against claims that their advice or design was negligent. It usually responds to claims made while the policy is in force.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you will hire advisers for wealth the way you hire consultants for buildings. On a building, you read the scope and the fee before you sign. Do the same here. Most problems with investment advice are not crimes; they are predictable results of how the adviser is paid and what standard of care the law imposes. Know those two things and most surprises disappear. This lesson teaches concepts only. Rules differ by jurisdiction and change; verify every point against the primary source before you rely on it.

Three standards of care

In plain English: some advisers must put your interest first, some must act in your best interest when they recommend something, and some need only recommend things that are not unsuitable for you.

The professional framing has three broad levels. A fiduciary duty is the highest: a duty of loyalty and care, requiring the adviser to act in your interest, avoid or fully manage conflicts, and not profit at your expense without informed consent. Discretionary managers, trustees and some registered advisers owe something close to this, depending on the jurisdiction and relationship. A best-interest standard requires the adviser, when recommending, to put your interest ahead of their own and to address conflicts, without necessarily owing an ongoing duty to monitor. A suitability standard asks only whether a recommendation fits your circumstances, goals and risk tolerance; among several suitable options, the adviser may legally pick the one that pays them more.

Several jurisdictions have moved their rules toward best-interest or conflict-centred obligations in recent years. Which standard applies to a particular adviser depends on their registration category and the service provided. Verify that against the primary source before you rely on it.

A worked example, hypothetical. Two products are both suitable for an investor. One costs 0.3 percent a year and pays the adviser nothing extra. The other costs 1.8 percent and pays the adviser an ongoing commission. Under a pure suitability standard, recommending the second may be permitted. Under a best-interest or fiduciary standard, the adviser must be able to justify why the costlier product serves the client better, and the conflict must be addressed, not merely mentioned.

How advisers are paid, and the conflict each method creates

In plain English: every way of paying an adviser pulls them in some direction. Your job is to know which direction.

The professional framing lists the common models. Commission: paid per product sold, which rewards selling and product choice. Asset-based fee: a percentage of money managed, which rewards gathering assets and can discourage advice to pay off debt or invest in your own business. Flat or hourly fee: paid for time or a plan, which reduces product bias but can reward selling more hours. Performance fee: a share of gains, which can reward risk-taking. No model is free of conflict. Fee-only does not mean conflict-free; it means the conflict has moved.

Say that out loud now.

A second worked example, hypothetical. An adviser charges 1 percent of assets. You have 1,500,000 dollars and ask whether to use 500,000 dollars to pay down a personal loan. If you do, the adviser's fee falls by 5,000 dollars a year. A professional adviser will still give you an honest answer, but you should notice the incentive and ask the question in a way that makes it easy for them to be honest, ideally of someone with no stake in the outcome.

Disclosure, know-your-client and records

Regulated advisers are typically required to collect information about your finances, goals and risk tolerance, often called know-your-client, and to assess whether recommendations fit. Many regimes also require disclosure of fees and compensation, sometimes in dollar terms in an annual report, and disclosure or management of material conflicts. Keep copies of every account agreement, fee schedule, risk profile and annual cost report. Vera's rule from Week 82 applies: a contemporaneous record of what you were told is worth more than your memory of it.

Two Systems

A conceptual comparison only; verify against primary source. In Canada, securities regulation is provincial and territorial, coordinated through a national umbrella of regulators, with self-regulatory organisations overseeing dealer firms. Registration categories determine what an adviser may do, and reforms in recent years strengthened conflict-of-interest and know-your-product obligations, with cost and compensation reporting to clients. In Guyana, securities activity is overseen by a national securities regulator under securities legislation, with a smaller market and fewer registered participants; banking and insurance fall under separate supervisors. The practical difference for you is depth: where the market is smaller, fewer local advisers are registered for complex products, and cross-border advice may be given by people not registered where you live. Confirm who regulates the person in front of you, and under which law, before you act.

Professional sign-off required: a lawyer for questions about the duty an adviser owes you, and a licensed, registered adviser for any actual investment decision.

Conflicts that are easy to miss

Some conflicts are obvious, like a commission. Others are built into the firm. A firm may recommend its own proprietary funds, earning both an advisory fee and a fund fee. It may receive revenue-sharing payments from outside fund companies for placing their products on its shelf. It may receive referral fees for introducing you to a lender, an insurer or a lawyer. An adviser may be rewarded internally for gathering assets into a particular product line. None of these is necessarily illegal; many must be disclosed or managed. Your defence is a simple written request at the start of any relationship.

Ask the adviser to confirm in writing: the standard of care that applies to each service; every form of compensation the adviser and the firm receive in connection with your account, in dollars where possible; whether any recommended product is managed by the firm or an affiliate; whether the firm receives any payment from a product provider; and who holds your assets. Keep the answer beside the account agreement. An adviser who will not answer these in writing has answered them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming everyone called an adviser owes you a fiduciary duty. The control is to ask, in writing, what standard of care applies to the service, how the adviser is paid in dollars, and what conflicts they have, and to keep the answers on file.

The beginner's mistake

Choosing an adviser on personality and returns, without reading the account agreement, the fee schedule and the registration category. The charm is the same under every standard; the obligation is not.

Callback

In Week 25, LEX and Vera taught you to start every professional relationship with an engagement letter that fixes scope, fees and who the professional acts for. An investment account agreement is that engagement letter for your money. Read it with the same discipline.

Recap

Fiduciary, best-interest and suitability are different duties. Every pay model creates a conflict; fee-only moves it rather than removing it. Know-your-client and fee disclosure protect you only if you read them and keep them. In Canada and Guyana, know who regulates the person advising you.

Next: Warrick on The Numbers: building a net-of-fee portfolio return and a rebalancing trade step by step.
checklist: I have asked in writing what standard of care applies to the service.
I know how my adviser is paid, in dollars, and by whom.
I know the adviser's registration category and who regulates them.
I have read the account agreement and fee schedule before signing.
I keep my know-your-client form, risk profile and annual cost reports on file.
I ask conflicted questions of someone with no stake in the answer.
A lawyer and a registered adviser are involved before any real decision.
head: Field checklist
speak: Not everyone called a financial adviser owes me the same duty. A fiduciary must act in my interest and avoid or manage conflicts. A best-interest standard requires an adviser, when recommending, to put my interest ahead of theirs. A suitability standard only requires that a recommendation fit me, so among suitable options the adviser may pick the one that pays them more. Which standard applies depends on registration and service, and I verify it against the primary source. Every pay model creates a pull: commissions reward selling, asset fees reward gathering assets and can discourage paying off debt, hourly fees reward hours, and performance fees reward risk. Fee-only moves the conflict; it does not remove it. In Canada regulation is provincial with national coordination; Guyana has a national securities regulator and a smaller market. I ask in writing, I keep the answers, and I involve a lawyer and a registered adviser before acting.
terms: Fiduciary duty — a legal duty of loyalty and care requiring a person to act in another's interest and to avoid or properly manage conflicts.
Suitability standard — an obligation only to recommend investments that fit the client's circumstances, goals and risk tolerance.
Know-your-client — the regulated process of collecting a client's financial information, goals and risk profile before advising.

hostile.q: I'm a fee-only adviser, so I have no conflicts. Why are you asking me to put my duty and my compensation in writing?
hostile.a: Because fee-only moves conflicts rather than removing them. If you charge on assets, your income falls if I pay down debt or put money into my own business. That does not make your advice wrong; it means I want the standard of care, the fee in dollars and the conflicts on file, so we both know the basis of every recommendation.

title: Net of Fees, Back to Target: A Portfolio Worked Step by Step
summary: This lesson builds a hypothetical three-class portfolio, calculates its expected return before and after every layer of cost, then runs a year of drift and works out the rebalancing trade. Every step has units.
body:
A portfolio's real return is the weighted return of its parts, minus every layer of cost, and its risk is controlled by trading back to written targets after the year has moved the weights. Both are simple arithmetic once you lay it out.

Recall

Q. What is an asset class?

A. A family of investments whose returns are driven by the same underlying forces, such as interest rates, company profits or rents.

Q. Why is a currency reserve sized by future obligations rather than by forecasts of the exchange rate?

A. Because the goal is to remove the mismatch between what you hold and what you owe, not to bet on where the currency goes. Matching obligations is a control; forecasting is a guess.

Q. What is an owner-controlled insurance program, often called an OCIP?

A. A single insurance program bought by the owner to cover the owner, contractor and subcontractors on a project, instead of each buying its own, giving one set of terms and often lower total cost.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, you already build pro formas line by line. A personal portfolio deserves the same treatment. Most people know their balance and their last year's return. Few know their expected net return after every fee, or the trade that would bring them back to plan. The calculation below takes ten minutes and changes how you read every statement afterward. All numbers are hypothetical, for arithmetic only, and recommend no product.

Step 1: the starting portfolio and its targets

A hypothetical investor holds 1,000,000 dollars outside their operating business, with a written policy:

ClassTarget weightDollarsAssumed gross returnProduct cost per year
Real estate fund40 percent400,0008 percent1.5 percent
Public equity index40 percent400,0007 percent0.1 percent
Short-term government bonds20 percent200,0004 percent0.1 percent

On top of the product costs, an adviser charges 0.75 percent a year on the whole portfolio. The policy allows each class to drift 5 percentage points either side of target before a rebalance.

Step 2: expected gross return

  1. Real estate: 0.40 times 8 percent equals 3.20 percent.
  2. Equity: 0.40 times 7 percent equals 2.80 percent.
  3. Bonds: 0.20 times 4 percent equals 0.80 percent.
  4. Weighted gross return: 3.20 plus 2.80 plus 0.80 equals 6.80 percent a year.

Step 3: every layer of cost

  1. Real estate product cost: 0.40 times 1.5 percent equals 0.60 percent.
  2. Equity product cost: 0.40 times 0.1 percent equals 0.04 percent.
  3. Bond product cost: 0.20 times 0.1 percent equals 0.02 percent.
  4. Weighted product cost: 0.66 percent.
  5. Advisory fee: 0.75 percent.
  6. Total cost: 0.66 plus 0.75 equals 1.41 percent a year.

In dollars, on 1,000,000 dollars, that is 14,100 dollars a year: 6,000 dollars to the real estate fund, 400 to the equity fund, 200 to the bond fund and 7,500 to the adviser.

Say that out loud now.

Step 4: expected net return

Net return equals 6.80 minus 1.41, which is 5.39 percent a year. Costs take 1.41 of 6.80 points, about 21 percent of the expected gross return. Notice that the real estate fund is 40 percent of the money but 0.60 of the 0.66 points of product cost, about 91 percent of it. That is the line to question first: what does it provide that a cheaper alternative, or your own direct real estate, does not? Remember the Day 3 warning: an appraisal-valued fund may look uncorrelated without being so.

Step 5: a year of drift

Suppose the year turns out like this, before costs, hypothetically: real estate gains 6 percent, equities fall 12 percent, bonds gain 4 percent. Ignore costs in this step to keep the drift clear.

  1. Real estate: 400,000 times 1.06 equals 424,000 dollars.
  2. Equity: 400,000 times 0.88 equals 352,000 dollars.
  3. Bonds: 200,000 times 1.04 equals 208,000 dollars.
  4. Total: 424,000 plus 352,000 plus 208,000 equals 984,000 dollars.

New weights: real estate 424,000 divided by 984,000 is about 43.1 percent; equity 352,000 divided by 984,000 is about 35.8 percent; bonds about 21.1 percent. Every class is still inside its 5-point band. Under the policy, no trade is required. That restraint matters: trading on every wobble costs money and invites second-guessing.

Step 6: a second year, and the rebalance

Year two, hypothetically: real estate gains 4 percent, equities fall another 15 percent, bonds gain 4 percent.

  1. Real estate: 424,000 times 1.04 equals 440,960 dollars.
  2. Equity: 352,000 times 0.85 equals 299,200 dollars.
  3. Bonds: 208,000 times 1.04 equals 216,320 dollars.
  4. Total: 956,480 dollars.
  5. Equity weight: 299,200 divided by 956,480 is about 31.3 percent, outside its 35 to 45 percent band.

The trade back to target:

  1. Equity target: 40 percent of 956,480 equals 382,592 dollars. Buy 382,592 minus 299,200, which is 83,392 dollars.
  2. Real estate target: 382,592 dollars. The fund holds 440,960, so it is over target by 58,368 dollars. If the fund cannot be redeemed quickly, the policy should say so, and the rebalance draws from the more liquid class.
  3. Bond target: 20 percent equals 191,296 dollars. Bonds hold 216,320, so sell 25,024 dollars.

If the real estate fund cannot be sold, the investor sells the 25,024 dollars of bonds and adds new money of 58,368 dollars, which together fund the 83,392 dollar equity purchase. This is the developer's version of rebalancing: illiquid holdings stay put, and new money does the work.

Step 7: what the cost line means over ten years

Run the cost line forward, because a percentage hides its size. Assume, hypothetically, the 5.39 percent net return holds for 10 years with no withdrawals.

  1. Growth factor: 1.0539 to the power of 10 is about 1.690.
  2. Ending value: 1,000,000 times 1.690 is about 1,690,000 dollars.

Now suppose the investor replaced the real estate fund with a cheaper real estate exposure, cutting total cost from 1.41 to 0.75 percent while gross return stays at 6.80 percent.

  1. Net return: 6.80 minus 0.75 equals 6.05 percent.
  2. Growth factor: 1.0605 to the power of 10 is about 1.799.
  3. Ending value: about 1,799,000 dollars.
  4. Difference: about 109,000 dollars over 10 years, from one line of the table.

That is the number to put in front of an adviser who recommends the expensive line. Not "fees are high", but "this line costs me about 109,000 dollars over ten years; show me what I get for it." The burden of proof sits on the fee.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a rebalancing rule that silently depends on selling something that cannot be sold. The control is to write in the policy which classes can actually be traded, on what notice, and how new money is directed when the illiquid class is over weight.

A note on the method itself. Every step above is arithmetic you can check on a phone calculator, and that is deliberate. If an adviser's statement cannot be reconciled to weights, returns and costs this simply, ask for the missing lines until it can. A portfolio you cannot reconcile is a portfolio you do not understand, and Mr Shabazz, you would never accept that from a contractor's payment application. Hold the statement to the same standard, every quarter, and keep the reconciliation with the statement.

The beginner's mistake

Calculating return gross of costs, and rebalancing on feel. Net return is the only return you keep, and a rule written before the year is the only defence against selling what has just fallen.

Callback

In Week 13, Sage built sources and uses so every dollar had a line and a purpose. Step 3 is the same discipline: each cost has a line, a dollar amount and someone who receives it. A cost without a line is a cost nobody is watching.

Recap

Weighted gross return, minus weighted product costs, minus advisory fees, gives net return: here 6.80 minus 1.41 equals 5.39 percent. Drift is measured against written bands. Rebalance only outside them, and plan for illiquid classes with new money. A licensed adviser is required before you act.

Next: Warrick in The Room: the meeting where an adviser pitches you a product, and the questions that expose the conflict.
checklist: I can compute my portfolio's weighted gross return.
I list every cost layer and total it as a percentage and in dollars.
I know which holding carries most of my cost.
My policy sets target weights and drift bands for each class.
My policy says which classes can actually be sold, and on what notice.
I direct new money to under-weight classes before selling anything.
I trade only when a band is breached, not on every move.
head: Field checklist
speak: A portfolio's net return is built in layers. Take each class's weight times its gross return and add them: here 40 percent real estate at 8, 40 percent equity at 7 and 20 percent bonds at 4 gives 6.8 percent. Then subtract every cost layer. The weighted product costs are 0.66 percent and the adviser takes 0.75, so total cost is 1.41 percent, or 14,100 dollars a year on a million. Net return is 5.39 percent. Most of the product cost came from one line, the real estate fund, so that is the first line to question. Then drift. After a year the weights move, and the policy says trade only if a class leaves its band. After two bad equity years, equity fell to about 31 percent, outside its band, so the plan buys about 83,000 dollars of equity. If the real estate fund cannot be sold, bonds and new money fund the trade.
terms: Weighted return — the sum of each holding's return multiplied by its share of the portfolio.
Drift band — the permitted range around a target weight before a rebalance is required.
Advisory fee — a charge for advice or management, usually a percentage of assets, paid on top of product costs.

hostile.q: Your rebalancing plan assumes you can sell the real estate fund. What happens if it suspends redemptions in the same year equities fall?
hostile.a: The plan does not rely on selling it. The policy lists it as illiquid, so when it is over weight we leave it and rebalance with the liquid classes and new money. In the worked case, 25,000 dollars of bonds and about 58,000 dollars of new money fund the equity purchase. If new money were not available, we would accept the wider drift rather than force a sale.

title: The Product Pitch: Finding the Conflict Without Starting a Fight
summary: A polished adviser recommends a product over lunch. This lesson scripts the meeting: the questions that surface fees and conflicts, the lines never to say, the question behind the question, and how to leave without committing. It closes with the monthly thread on working with advisers.
body:
In a product pitch, your job is not to judge the product in the room. It is to surface three facts, how the adviser is paid, what the total cost is and who holds the assets, and then to leave without committing.

Recall

Q. In the Madoff case, what structural feature was the root cause for investors?

A. The same firm managed the money, executed the trades, held the assets and produced the statements, so no independent party could confirm the assets existed.

Q. In a wealth architecture, why separate operating assets from personal reserves?

A. So a failure in the business cannot reach the reserves meant to carry you and your obligations through that failure.

Q. What is a letter of credit used for on a construction project?

A. A bank's promise to pay a named beneficiary on presentation of specified documents, often used as security for performance or deposits in place of cash.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, as your projects succeed you will be approached often. The approaches will be pleasant, well prepared and flattering. Most will come from honest people working inside a pay structure that pulls them toward certain products. You do not need to distrust them. You need a routine that surfaces the facts every time, so your decision rests on evidence rather than on the warmth of the lunch.

The scene

A hypothetical scene. A senior adviser from a well-known firm has asked for lunch. She has prepared a presentation for a private real estate income fund: steady distributions, low reported volatility, and a minimum investment of 250,000 dollars. She knows your background and says the fund "speaks your language". She is fluent, likeable and specific.

The lines to say

  • "Thank you. Before we go through the strategy, help me with three practical points."
  • "If I invest 250,000 dollars, what is the total annual cost to me in dollars, including every fee in the fund and any fee to you or your firm?"
  • "How are you paid if I invest, and does that change between this fund and the alternatives you could offer?"
  • "Who holds the assets, in whose name, and who prepares the valuations and the statements?"
  • "How is the property valued, how often, and by whom?"
  • "Under what conditions can I get my money out, and has the fund ever limited withdrawals?"
  • "Please send me the offering document, the fee schedule and the last audited financial statements. I'll review them with my own adviser and come back to you."

Each question is neutral and factual. None accuses her. Each one, answered in writing, becomes part of your record.

The lines never to say

  • "I trust you, just tell me where to put it." That hands over the decision and the record.
  • "I know real estate better than most, so I don't need the details." Your expertise in building is not expertise in how a fund is valued, charged and redeemed.
  • "Let's do it, I'll sign today." Nothing good about an investment disappears in a week.
  • "Are you trying to rip me off?" It ends the meeting and teaches you nothing.

Say that out loud now.

The question behind the question

When she says "it speaks your language", the question behind it is whether familiarity will replace analysis. You already have large real estate exposure through your projects. The real question is whether this adds a different return driver or doubles down on the one you have, at a higher fee. Ask it out loud: "My wealth is already concentrated in real estate. Show me how this behaves differently from what I already own." If the answer is the smooth line on the chart, remember Day 1: appraisal-based values move slowly, and smoothness can be a feature of the reporting rather than of the asset.

When she says "the minimum closes at the end of the month", the question behind it is urgency. Urgency is the most common pressure tactic in selling, and Kema taught you in Week 3 how scarcity distorts judgement. Answer calmly: "If it closes before my review is done, it wasn't for me."

When to stay silent

After you ask how she is paid, stop talking and let her answer fully. Do not fill the pause with "of course, everyone has to make a living". The pause is where the real answer arrives. Stay silent again when she gives the total cost; write the number down before you react to it.

Holding your state

Flattery and good food lower your guard more than any argument. Decide before the lunch that you will not commit in the room, and say so early: "I never decide at a first meeting." It removes the pressure for both of you. If you feel the pull to say yes, notice it, name it to yourself, and return to your three facts. Your composure here is the same one you use in a lender meeting: slow pace, short sentences, a written list.

Working with advisers: the monthly thread

Advisers are tools, and a tool has a scope. Hire each one for a defined job, in writing, with its pay model and duty stated. Keep at least one adviser whose pay does not depend on what you buy, and use that person to review the recommendations of those whose pay does. That is not suspicion; it is the same separation of design and checking you use on a building.

Review every adviser once a year on three questions: did their advice serve your written plan, what did it cost in dollars, and did they ever tell you something you did not want to hear? An adviser who never disagrees with you is not advising. Record the answers in your decision journal, the habit Kema set in Week 2.

If she pushes back

Sometimes an adviser will treat factual questions as an insult, or answer a different question. Keep your tone level and repeat the question once, in the same words. "I understand. What is the total annual cost in dollars on 250,000?" If the answer is a percentage of the fund's net asset value, ask her to convert it in writing. If she says the figure depends on performance, ask for the figure at the fund's last reported return. If she says custody is "with our trust company", note that the firm and the custodian are affiliated and ask whether an independent administrator prepares the valuations.

After the meeting, read the documents in a fixed order: the fee section, the redemption and suspension section, the valuation policy, the conflicts section, and only then the strategy. Most people read in the reverse order and are persuaded before they reach the parts that decide the outcome. Write down, in your decision journal, what you expect to be true if you invest and what would make you sell. Review it with an adviser whose pay does not depend on your answer.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is committing in the room under warmth and urgency. The control is a standing rule, announced at the start, that you never decide at a first meeting, plus three facts in writing before any decision: pay, total cost and custody.

The beginner's mistake

Arguing about the strategy, which the adviser knows better, instead of asking about pay, cost and custody, which decide most of the outcome and which she must answer plainly.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the "I'll confirm by Friday" move: a commitment to respond, not to agree. Here it becomes "I'll review this with my own adviser and come back to you." It ends the meeting gracefully and protects the decision.

Recap

Ask three things: how she is paid, the total cost in dollars, and who holds and values the assets. Ask whether the product adds a different driver to what you already own. Stay silent after hard questions. Never decide at a first meeting.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: six questions, a Red Pen drill and a boardroom drill on assets beyond real estate.
checklist: I announce at the start that I never decide at a first meeting.
I ask the total annual cost in dollars, including every layer.
I ask how the adviser is paid and whether pay differs across alternatives.
I ask who holds the assets and who values and reports them.
I ask how the product differs from what I already own.
I request the offering document, fee schedule and audited statements.
I keep one adviser whose pay does not depend on what I buy.
head: Field checklist
speak: In a product pitch I am not there to judge the strategy. I am there to surface three facts: how the adviser is paid, the total annual cost in dollars, and who holds and values the assets. I open by saying I never decide at a first meeting, which removes the pressure. I ask how the product behaves differently from the real estate I already own, because familiarity is not diversification, and smooth appraisal-based returns can be a reporting effect. After I ask about pay, I stay silent and let the answer arrive. I treat a closing deadline as pressure, not information. I ask for the offering document, fee schedule and audited statements, and say I will review them with my own adviser. Over time, I keep at least one adviser whose pay does not depend on what I buy, and I review every adviser once a year on value, cost and candour.
terms: Offering document — the legal document describing an investment's terms, fees, risks and rights, given to prospective investors.
Redemption terms — the conditions, notice periods and limits under which an investor can withdraw money from a fund.
Pressure tactic — a selling technique, such as an artificial deadline, designed to shorten a buyer's analysis.

hostile.q: You've asked about my pay three different ways. Are you suggesting I'm not acting in your interest?
hostile.a: Not at all. I ask every adviser the same three questions, because pay, cost and custody decide most of the outcome and I want them on file before I decide anything. You've been clear and helpful. Please send the fee schedule and the audited statements, and I'll come back to you after my review.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 87 Review: What You Own Beyond Your Projects
summary: Six questions on asset classes, correlation, fees and conflicts of interest, a recap of the week, a Red Pen drill on a hypothetical investment recommendation, and a two-minute boardroom drill.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: own things that answer to different forces, know every fee in dollars, and never let the person who reports your wealth also control it.

Recall

Q. In the Day 3 example, how much did a 1.75 point fee difference cost over 25 years on 1,000,000 dollars?

A. About 1,730,000 dollars, roughly a third of the final value, on hypothetical numbers with the same gross return.

Q. What is a liquidity tier?

A. A group of assets sorted by how quickly it becomes cash without a forced discount, from immediate cash to assets that take years.

Q. What is the difference between a performance bond and a payment bond?

A. A performance bond protects the owner if the contractor fails to complete the work. A payment bond protects subcontractors and suppliers if the contractor fails to pay them.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, wealth outside your projects is where your discipline is least tested and your exposure is easiest to forget. If you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit with any adviser as an informed client. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. How do you define an asset class?

Answer: By what drives its return, not by its label. Cash follows short-term rates, bonds follow rates and credit, equities follow company profits, real estate follows rents, cap rates and credit.

Question 2. What does correlation measure, and what are its two traps?

Answer: How much two investments move together, from minus one to plus one. It rises in a crisis, and appraisal-based assets look less correlated than they are because their values update slowly.

Question 3. Why does a fee do more damage than its size suggests?

Answer: It is charged every year, good or bad, and the money taken never compounds for you again.

Question 4. Name the three standards of care an adviser may owe.

Answer: Fiduciary duty, best-interest, and suitability. Which applies depends on registration and the service, and must be verified against the primary source.

Question 5. What was the structural root cause in the Madoff case?

Answer: One firm managed, executed, held and reported the money, so nothing independent confirmed the assets existed.

Question 6. How does a developer rebalance when his largest asset is illiquid?

Answer: By directing new money, such as profits and distributions, to under-weight classes under a written policy, rather than selling buildings.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Warrick defined asset classes by their drivers and introduced correlation and rebalancing. Ford and Roman took the Madoff fraud through seven steps, giving Rule 87 on separating manager, custodian and record keeper. Warrick priced fees and correlation in dollars. REGA explained fiduciary, best-interest and suitability standards, pay models and conflicts, with Canada and Guyana compared. Warrick built a net-of-fee portfolio and a rebalancing trade. Warrick ran the product pitch.

The Red Pen

Read this hypothetical recommendation memo from an adviser and find the defects before reading on.

Recommendation. Given your real estate expertise, we recommend placing 600,000 dollars, about half your liquid reserve, in our firm's Private Property Income Fund. The fund has produced steady returns with very low volatility and is uncorrelated with markets. Fees are competitive. Assets are held by our affiliated trust company and valuations are prepared by our internal team. Redemptions are generally available. This recommendation is suitable for your profile.

The defects. First, it adds more real estate to an investor already concentrated in real estate, and calls it a fit because of expertise, which is familiarity, not diversification. Second, half the liquid reserve in an illiquid fund breaks the liquidity floor. Third, "very low volatility" and "uncorrelated" are claimed without saying the values come from appraisal or internal estimates, which smooth the line. Fourth, "fees are competitive" gives no total cost in dollars. Fifth, custody sits with an affiliate and valuation is internal, so the firm controls the assets and the reporting, the Rule 87 failure in miniature. Sixth, "generally available" redemptions hide the conditions under which they are limited. Seventh, "suitable" names the lowest standard of care and says nothing about the firm's own pay from its own fund.

The boardroom drill

Explain the week in two minutes, as if to a business partner who asks, "We're making good money. Where should the profit go that isn't the next project?" Then compare with this model.

Model answer: "First, a rule: we count return drivers, not holdings. Most of our wealth answers to interest rates, credit and local demand, so more property, even in different buildings, is the same bet. Money outside the business should sit in classes driven by different forces, under a written policy with target weights and ranges, funded from distributions. Second, fees. A fee compounds against us every year, so we price every holding's total cost in dollars and pay more only for proven, net-of-fee value. Third, conflicts. Every adviser is paid in a way that pulls them somewhere, so we get their standard of care, their pay and custody arrangements in writing. And we never hold anything where the manager, the custodian and the record keeper are the same party. A licensed adviser signs off before we act."

Score yourself. Did you lead with the bottom line? Did you distinguish holdings from drivers? Did you mention fees in dollars and conflicts in writing? Did you state Rule 87? Did you finish inside two minutes?

Common wrong answers

Kema's notes on where people slip. On Question 1, the common error is naming asset classes by product, such as "funds" or "private equity", rather than by driver. Private equity is mostly equity exposure with less liquidity and more fees. On Question 2, people define correlation correctly and forget both traps; the traps are the point. On Question 3, people say fees are high; the stronger answer explains compounding and the fact that a fee is charged in bad years too. On Question 4, people assume every professional owes a fiduciary duty. On Question 5, people say "Madoff lied". He did, but the investor's lesson is structural: lies survive where nobody independent can check. On Question 6, people say "sell some property". A developer usually cannot, and should not plan to.

If you missed two or more, reread Day 1 and Day 4 before tomorrow, then answer again aloud. Kema's standard is not memorising the answers. It is being able to explain each one to someone who disagrees, in your own words, at the pace you would use in a lender meeting.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is false comfort: many holdings, smooth returns and a trusted name standing in for real diversification, known costs and independent custody. The control is the three-column Wealth Ledger, cost, driver and valuation method, reviewed every year.

A second drill for the week, if you have five more minutes. Take one real statement you receive, any investment account, and fill in the three Wealth Ledger columns for each line: total annual cost in dollars, return driver, and valuation method. Do not change anything yet. Simply look at how many lines share the same driver, and which line carries most of the cost. Bring the result to your adviser with one question: "What would this look like if it matched my written plan?" Note the answer in your decision journal and date it.

The beginner's mistake

Studying which product is best instead of learning the questions that expose any product's cost, conflict and custody.

Callback

In Week 72, REGA and Cole taught know-your-client from the bank's side: source of funds, beneficial ownership, reputation. This week turns it around. You now run know-your-adviser and know-your-custodian with the same rigour a bank applies to you.

Recap

Asset classes by driver. Correlation by evidence. Fees in dollars. Duties and pay in writing. Custody independent. Rule 87 holds it all together.

head: The six questions
speak: This week was about the wealth I hold outside my projects. Asset classes are defined by what drives their return, and diversification comes from different drivers, not more holdings. Correlation measures whether assets move together; it rises in a crisis, and appraisal-based assets look smoother than they are. Fees compound against me every year, so I price each holding's total cost in dollars. Advisers may owe a fiduciary duty, a best-interest standard or only suitability, and every pay model creates a pull, so I get duty, pay and conflicts in writing. The Madoff case gave Rule 87: never invest where the manager, custodian and record keeper are the same party, and check the auditor myself. Because my largest asset is illiquid, I rebalance by directing new money under a written policy. A licensed adviser reviews everything before I act.
terms: Strategic asset allocation — written long-term target weights for each asset class, with permitted ranges.
Liquidity floor — the minimum readily available cash and near-cash a person will not go below.
Independent custody — assets held by a separate institution, in the investor's name, that confirms them directly.

hostile.q: You keep talking about diversification, but real estate has made you wealthy. Why would you put money anywhere you don't have an edge?
hostile.a: Because my edge is in making money, not in surviving the year my one market turns. My projects, guarantees and income already answer to the same forces. Holding some wealth in classes driven by different forces is what lets me keep the edge, by not having to sell into a downturn. The amount is set in a written policy with a licensed adviser, not by feel.
